topics.title: Getting started
topics.html:
Getting started

SpectraSuite is an offline-first desktop analysis environment. Choose an available workspace on Home, import a numeric file or open a saved spectroscopy session, inspect the selected X and Y columns, then work in the plot, table and analysis views. Scientific data is processed locally; update discovery is a separate optional network function.

Workspace basics

The single-window application keeps Home, import and analysis documents in one project shell. Select a document to change the active context. The ribbon presents Home, Data, Plot, Process, Analyze, Annotate, View, Export, Learn and Help; available commands depend on the active document. The project explorer organizes datasets and documents, while Results and History expose derived output and recorded operations. A recorded history is not an independent record of laboratory acquisition or instrument calibration.

First analysis checklist

  1. Choose the correct technique and check its maturity label.
  2. Import data and confirm X/Y roles, axes and units.
  3. Inspect raw curves before applying processing.
  4. Record parameters, selected regions and assumptions.
  5. Inspect results and export figures or data using the relevant workspace commands.

Keep an original copy of experimental measurements. Do not use preview workspaces as validated quantitative techniques without independent checks.

topics.title: Importing data
topics.html:
Importing data

The spectroscopy reader accepts common numeric text formats including CSV, TSV, TXT, XY, DAT, DPT, ASR and RAW, and Excel XLSX/XLS. Shared import also recognizes ASC in selected workflows. The importer discovers numeric columns, multiple workbook sheets, repeated X/Y pairs and shared-X multiple-Y tables; review the dataset chooser when multiple candidates are found.

  1. Select Home or Data import, or drop supported files onto a compatible workspace.
  2. Check delimiters, decimal notation, headers and numeric values.
  3. Select the intended dataset and inspect axis names and units.
  4. Use Data Table to verify that sample order and numeric values make sense.

Typical data are two columns: independent variable X and measured signal Y. A file extension alone does not guarantee that vendor-specific binary contents can be parsed. LIBS offers folder/ZIP import; 3D/Fluid have additional format-specific constraints.

Troubleshooting

If a plot is blank, verify that a numeric dataset was selected, valid X/Y columns exist and axis limits contain the points. If a file is rejected, export a plain numeric CSV from the instrument's software and retry.

topics.title: Workspace and ribbon
topics.html:
Workspace and ribbon

The persistent SpectraSuite window contains a project/data explorer, central document workspace and contextual ribbon. Spectroscopy uses Plot and Data Table views, with Inspector, Results and History available for the active analysis. Multiple open analyses should retain independent active-document settings.

Plot controls

Use the Matplotlib toolbar for home/reset, back/forward, pan, zoom and saving when exposed. Plot/axis properties manage labels, limits, styles and legends. The Annotate tools support text, arrows and shapes with editing and history actions. Select datasets deliberately before applying processing or measurements.

Sessions and exports

Spectroscopy sessions use JSON and are intended to preserve supported analysis state. Before relying on a reopened project, verify datasets, transformations, displayed units and results. Export options include vector PDF/SVG and raster PNG/JPG/TIFF, processed CSV and batch/report outputs where supported. An option to trim empty outer margins can change the exported dimensions; disable it when exact dimensions are required.

Updates and appearance

Update checking uses public GitHub Releases and does not install software automatically. The appearance theme changes interface accents but should not recolor scientific curves or figure exports. Check release-channel preferences before opting into test builds.

topics.title: FT-IR
topics.html:
FT-IR spectroscopy

Phenomenon: infrared absorption excites vibrational transitions whose transition dipole moment changes. Vibrations and group frequencies depend on molecular structure, bonding and environment.

Instrument: IR source → Michelson interferometer → sample → detector → interferogram → Fourier transform → spectrum. Reference/background measurements correct optical and atmospheric contributions but do not eliminate all artifacts.

Imported data: wavenumber (cm⁻¹) versus transmittance (%), absorbance or instrument signal. The conventional wavenumber axis decreases left to right. Absorbance A = −log₁₀(T), where T is fractional transmittance (not percentage); T = %T / 100.

In SpectraSuite: inspect multiple curves using individual/overlay/stack/grid layouts, ALS or manual baseline correction, smoothing, normalization, derivatives, reference subtraction, FT-IR valley selection, selected-range area, Gaussian component fitting and annotations. The peak detector works downward for ordinary transmittance spectra and upward after conversion to absorbance.

Interpretation: a candidate functional-group band is an aid, not proof of chemical identity. Intensities depend on sample thickness, concentration, sampling mode and baseline. Over-smoothing, atmospheric H₂O/CO₂, ATR effects, overlapping bands and improper transmission-to-absorbance conventions are frequent sources of error.

topics.title: XRD
topics.html:
X-ray diffraction

Phenomenon: coherent scattering from periodic crystal planes creates diffraction maxima when Bragg's condition nλ = 2d sin θ is met. Here d is lattice-plane spacing, λ the X-ray wavelength, θ the Bragg angle, and the diffractometer generally records 2θ (degrees).

Instrument: X-ray tube/source → optics → specimen/goniometer → detector → counts or intensity versus 2θ.

In SpectraSuite: upward peak selection, peak labels, local FWHM and a simple Scherrer crystallite-size estimate. The implementation uses D = Kλ/(β cos θ) with K=0.9 and λ=0.15406 nm, converting a FWHM expressed in 2θ degrees to radians; θ is half the 2θ peak position. D is expressed in nm with these wavelength units. Check the source workflow and instrument wavelength before using the numeric result.

Important: coherent-domain (crystallite) size is not necessarily physical particle size. Instrumental width, microstrain, defects, overlapping peaks, shape-factor assumptions and profile shapes can broaden peaks. Automatic instrumental broadening correction, Williamson–Hall, phase identification and Rietveld refinement are not established working features in the inspected source; do not assume they were applied.

topics.title: UV-Vis
topics.html:
UV–visible spectroscopy

Phenomenon: photons excite electronic transitions, measured as wavelength-dependent transmission, reflection or absorption. A typical instrument uses UV/visible source(s), a monochromator or dispersive element, sample optics and detector.

Observable: sample and reference intensity determine fractional transmittance T = I/I₀ and absorbance A = −log₁₀ T. Beer–Lambert A = εcl is conditional on a suitable linear absorbing system with defined path length, concentration and negligible scattering.

In SpectraSuite: wavelength to photon energy uses E(eV) = 1239.841984 / λ(nm). Absorbance becomes α(cm⁻¹) = 2.302585093 A / (thickness in μm × 10⁻⁴) only when positive film thickness is supplied; otherwise a relative absorption proxy is used. Kubelka–Munk for reflectance uses F(R)=(1−R)²/(2R), with R fractional reflectance. These proxies are not automatically validated absolute absorption coefficients.

Tauc: the transform is (αE)^r with r = 2 (direct allowed), 1/2 (indirect allowed), 2/3 (direct forbidden) or 1/3 (indirect forbidden) in current code. Fit a researcher-reviewed positive-slope linear interval: Eg = −intercept/slope. The code reports R² and warnings, including R² below 0.98. These are fit diagnostics, not proof of the transition mechanism. Urbach analysis fits ln(absorption) versus energy with EU = 1/slope for positive slope.

Limitations: fit-window selection, scattering, substrate, thickness, reflection assumptions, low-signal edges and transition model affect conclusions. The preprocessing helper can conservatively trim noisy edges, at most a configured fraction, and does not replace raw-data inspection.

topics.title: Raman
topics.html:
Raman spectroscopy

Phenomenon: most elastically scattered photons are Rayleigh scattered; a small fraction exchanges energy with vibrational modes (Raman scattering). Stokes photons have lower energy than the laser, while anti-Stokes photons have higher energy.

Instrument: monochromatic excitation laser → sample → collection optics → Rayleigh-rejection filters → spectrograph → detector. Displayed Raman shift is typically cm⁻¹, not absolute emitted wavelength.

In SpectraSuite: Raman uses shared processing, peak detection, FWHM, a locally integrated FWHM-interval area, Gaussian fitting and ratios of two distinct detected peak heights. The peak ratio helper uses target shifts and a default matching tolerance of 10 cm⁻¹; a missing or same selected band raises an error. The local area is baseline-relative and is not total band area.

Limitations: fluorescence, laser heating, sample orientation, detector response and overlapping bands complicate interpretation. Do not infer stoichiometry, phase identity or concentration from a raw ratio without calibration and experimental controls.

topics.title: XPS (preview)
topics.html:
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy — experimental preview

Phenomenon: photoelectric emission from surface atoms. The electron analyzer measures kinetic energy; binding energy is commonly estimated as EB = hν − EK − φ for a consistent analyzer referencing convention.

Instrument: X-ray source → sample in high vacuum → electrostatic electron-energy analyzer → detector → photoelectron spectrum. Survey scans inspect broad elemental signals; high-resolution windows are used to investigate chemical shifts and environments. Charging and referencing are crucial.

In SpectraSuite: generic intensity versus binding-energy plotting, a conventionally decreasing eV axis, generic peak/area tools, processing, overlays, annotations, sessions and export. It is a preview, not a chemically complete XPS interpretation engine.

Not implemented as validated XPS workflows: VAMAS parsing, charge calibration, Shirley/Tougaard background subtraction, constrained chemical-state fits, sensitivity-factor correction and atomic-percent quantification. A generic fitted peak is not a chemical-state assignment.

topics.title: LIBS (preview)
topics.html:
Laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy — experimental preview

Phenomenon: a focused high-intensity laser pulse ablates the target and generates a transient plasma. Excited atoms and ions emit characteristic photons as the plasma cools.

Instrument: pulsed laser → target/plasma → collection optics → spectrometer → gated or ungated detector → emission intensity versus wavelength (usually nm).

In SpectraSuite: import numeric LIBS spectra and select many spectra from folders or ZIP archives, use generic peaks/areas, compare datasets and export. Raw signal is preserved by default. No automated elemental identification or concentration calculation is claimed.

Limits: line overlaps, self-absorption, plasma conditions, matrix effects, atmospheric lines, detector response and wavelength calibration matter. Quantitative LIBS needs validated standards and a calibration strategy. Electron density and plasma temperature workflows are not currently implemented.

topics.title: Baseline and ALS
topics.html:
Baseline correction and ALS

Purpose: estimate slowly varying background so band shape and integrated intensity can be inspected. A poor baseline changes peak heights, widths and areas.

Asymmetric least squares: seek a smooth baseline z by minimizing Σwᵢ(yᵢ−zᵢ)² + λΣ(Δ²zᵢ)², iteratively adjusting weights for observations above and below z. The processing helper defines baseline_als(y, lam=10⁸, p=0.05, itermax=10); the per-spectrum interface stores als_lam as a base-10 logarithm and uses lam=10 ** als_lam (default 8.0), p default 0.05.

In processing order: Savitzky–Golay smoothing if enabled, then baseline subtraction if enabled, then derivatives if selected. The input Y is copied in process_spectrum; inspect session/workspace state before claiming unconditional recovery across every workflow.

Use with care: peak crowding, asymmetric envelopes and strong background changes can make the baseline physically implausible. Preserve raw measurements and export settings alongside processed results.

topics.title: Smoothing and derivatives
topics.html:
Savitzky–Golay smoothing and derivatives

A local polynomial is fitted within a moving window to reduce high-frequency noise while retaining polynomial-like curve structure. Smoothing can still suppress narrow peaks or shift extrema if the window is too large.

In SpectraSuite's process_spectrum helper: smooth defaults to 0 (off). When positive, the requested window is forced odd and at least five samples; polynomial order is 3; the transform is applied only when data length exceeds the window. First and second derivatives use Savitzky–Golay order 3, the selected smoothing window or 5 if smoothing is off, with derivative order 1 or 2. The function does not specify a wavelength/sample-spacing delta, so these derivatives are with respect to sample index unless another workflow rescales them.

Scientific caution: sample spacing, noisy boundaries and nonuniform X matter. Compare processed and raw curves, and avoid treating a smoothed signal as a better experimental measurement merely because it looks cleaner.

topics.title: Reference subtraction and trimming
topics.html:
Reference subtraction and noisy-edge trimming

Reference subtraction removes a separately measured component only when acquisition modes, units and signal scales are compatible. In spectral_preprocessing.subtract_reference the reference is sorted in X, interpolated onto the sample X positions and subtracted with a configurable multiplier (default 1). NumPy interpolation uses boundary values outside the reference range; overlapping domains should be checked before interpreting the result.

The optical trim_noisy_edges helper compares local end-region point-to-point variation against a central robust noise scale; its default maximum_fraction is 0.10 and curves under 50 finite points are returned untrimmed. It may discard suspect edge samples, so retain original measurement files and verify that meaningful spectral structure was not removed.

topics.title: Peak detection, area and FWHM
topics.html:
Peak detection, area and FWHM

A local maximum/minimum is a feature of the supplied processed signal, not a chemical assignment. The shared detector smooths a copy for detection, estimates robust span and derivative noise, and uses prominence at least max(0.08 × robust span, 6 × noise, machine epsilon) when prominence is automatic. Conventional FT-IR transmittance valleys are detected downward; other workflows predominantly detect upward features.

FWHM: the distance between the two half-height crossings, after defining the peak and baseline. Widths must be converted to physical X units rather than conflated with sample indices. Peak area is an integral over a specified interval, often via numerical trapezoids; units are signal × X unit and results depend on baseline, clipping and interval.

Raman specific: peak_widths uses relative height 0.5, with interpolation of crossings onto X. The local area is trapezoidal integration of the positive signal above a straight baseline connecting those crossings. It is not full-band area.

topics.title: Scherrer estimate
topics.html:
Scherrer crystallite-size calculation

Equation: D = Kλ/(β cos θ). D is the coherent diffraction-domain size; K is dimensionless shape factor; λ and D share the same length unit; β is broadening in radians of 2θ; and θ is half the peak position angle. For λ = 0.15406 nm and K = 0.9, D is in nm.

In the source snapshot the XRD workflow is a simple FWHM-based Scherrer estimate. It does not automatically remove instrumental broadening or strain broadening, and the result should not be called measured particle diameter. Compare instrument standards, line-shape corrections and several reflections independently before making structural claims.

Reference: Patterson, A. L. (1939), The Scherrer Formula for X-Ray Particle Size Determination, Physical Review 56, 978–982.

topics.title: Tauc and Urbach
topics.html:
Tauc and Urbach analysis

The Tauc model linearizes an assumed absorption-edge relation. SpectraSuite constructs (αE)^r with transition-specific exponent r and fits ordinate = mE + b. The extrapolated energy intercept is Eg = −b/m. Current code rejects non-positive slopes and non-physical intercepts, reports R² and a propagated regression uncertainty where obtainable, and warns on poorly linear or excessive-extrapolation intervals.

Urbach energy follows α(E) ∝ exp(E/EU) over an appropriate exponential tail; fit ln α versus E and compute EU = 1/m for positive slope. The relative-absorption proxy, diffuse-reflectance transform and selected energy interval may invalidate naive comparisons between samples.

References: Tauc, J., Grigorovici, R., and Vancu, A. (1966), Physica Status Solidi 15, 627–637; Urbach, F. (1953), Physical Review 92, 1324.

topics.title: Deconvolution and fitting
topics.html:
Peak fitting and deconvolution

Fitting approximates the observed signal as baseline plus parameterized peaks. A Gaussian curve is y(x)=A exp[−(x−μ)²/(2σ²)] with FWHM = 2√(2 ln 2)σ. Lorentzian and Voigt families reflect different tail and broadening assumptions; their scientific introduction does not establish that a corresponding SpectraSuite fitter exists.

Implemented scope: Gaussian component fitting/deconvolution is documented in shared FT-IR, UV-Vis and Raman workflows. Do not claim Lorentzian, Voigt or pseudo-Voigt fitting as working until source and tests confirm it.

Interpretation: components can be mathematically nonunique. Choose plausible model complexity, fit region and background, inspect residuals, and do not equate a fitted component with an independently confirmed species.

topics.title: From instrument to interpretation
topics.html:
From measurement to interpretation

Physical phenomenon → instrument measurement → imported X/Y data → processing → quantitative analysis → scientific interpretation.

The instrument converts a physical response into detector signals and instrument software may already transform or normalize them. Confirm whether a file is raw counts, transmittance, absorbance, diffraction intensity, photoelectron counts or plasma emission. SpectraSuite reads and analyzes supplied datasets; it does not control the instrument or reconstruct missing calibration/metadata.

Processing is not a new experimental measurement. Fit accuracy is not necessarily physical validity. Record the original data, preparation, instrument settings, sample geometry, processing parameters, fit interval, units and uncertainty sources when drawing conclusions.

topics.title: Equations and sources
topics.html:
Equations and scientific references

Bragg: nλ=2d sinθ (λ,d lengths; θ half of diffraction 2θ).

Scherrer: D=Kλ/(β cosθ); broadening β in radians, K dimensionless.

Absorbance: A=−log₁₀ T, T fractional transmittance.

Kubelka–Munk: F(R)=(1−R)²/(2R), R fractional diffuse reflectance, subject to scattering and optical-model assumptions.

Tauc: fit (αE)^r = mE+b, Eg=−b/m under assumed transition and valid edge region.

Urbach: lnα = E/EU + constant in selected tail region.

Gaussian: A exp[−(x−μ)²/(2σ²)].

Further reading

  1. Griffiths & de Haseth, Fourier Transform Infrared Spectrometry, 2nd ed., Wiley (2007).
  2. Cullity & Stock, Elements of X-Ray Diffraction, 3rd ed., Prentice Hall (2001).
  3. Patterson (1939), Physical Review 56, 978–982.
  4. Hollas, Modern Spectroscopy, 4th ed., Wiley (2004).
  5. Tauc et al. (1966), Physica Status Solidi 15, 627–637.
  6. Urbach (1953), Physical Review 92, 1324.
  7. Savitzky & Golay (1964), Analytical Chemistry 36, 1627–1639.
  8. Eilers & Boelens (2005), Baseline Correction with Asymmetric Least Squares, Leiden University report.
  9. Brundle, Evans & Wilson (eds.), Encyclopedia of Materials Characterization, Butterworth-Heinemann (1992).
  10. Cremers & Radziemski, Handbook of Laser-Induced Breakdown Spectroscopy, 2nd ed., Wiley (2013).

These works explain underlying science; implementations and defaults must be checked against SpectraSuite code rather than inferred from textbooks.
